```gherkin
Scenario: Edge case - a story covered only manually
  Given US-VP-006 naked POC carry-forward has only manual coverage
  Then the document states this explicitly, records the manual execution evidence, and files an automation follow-up ticket rather than implying automated coverage

Scenario: Contract freeze is demonstrated, not asserted
  Given a deliberate breaking change to the ProfileUpdate schema on a scratch branch
  When CI runs
  Then the contract tests fail, and the evidence is linked from the sign-off document

Scenario: Owner acceptance is recorded
  When the epic is demoed at a sprint review
  Then explicit owner acceptance is recorded in the ticket with a date, per the epic Definition of Done
```

## Technical notes / design
- The document is assembled from links to primary evidence rather than restating numbers, with one exception: the performance verdicts and the coverage figures are copied in, because a gate reviewer must not have to open six tabs to see whether the epic passed.
- The metric publication statement is the highest-leverage part: later epics will treat `profile_poc` as ground truth, so this ticket verifies the published values against the `E19-Q02` oracle one final time on the release candidate build, not on an old CI run.

title: Composite and per-session multiple profiles served from the cold tier
body:
## Context
Implements **US-VP-003 — Composite / multi-period profiles (Should)**. Longer-term value only shows up when sessions are merged, and "per session, side by side" multiples are how traders compare successive days' acceptance. The NFR binds this story to the storage tier: "composite queries served from the **cold tier (Parquet/DuckDB)** within 2 s for 30 sessions", and the third scenario makes recorder coverage a first-class product behaviour rather than an error: "the composite is built from what exists and **states the covered range explicitly**".

## Scope / Deliverables
- `split=composite`: N selected sessions merged into one profile — summed element-wise **before** POC/VA computation (`24-internal-schemas.md` §5.2: "Composites never average; they accumulate"), with its own POC and value area.
- `split=session` multiples: one profile per session drawn at its own time position on the chart's time axis, each with its own POC/VA.
- Composite anchors in **SCR-039**: session / day / week / custom range picker, plus look-back count.
- Cold-tier query path: Parquet/DuckDB for windows outside hot retention, `meta.sources` reporting the mix; progress indication rather than a frozen pane for long look-backs (SCR-039 perf note).
- Coverage honesty: covered range stated in the legend, the partial-history chip when the recorder covers fewer sessions than requested, and a warning (not a block) when the requested look-back exceeds recorded history (SCR-039 validation).

## Out of scope
- Recorder retention policy and Parquet export itself — **E16**; this story consumes the cold tier.
- Automatic "composite of the current balance area" detection — **E25**.
- Cross-symbol composites.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Composite of N sessions
  When I select the last 5 sessions
  Then one merged profile is drawn with its own POC and value area

Scenario: Multiples
  When I choose "per session, side by side"
  Then each session gets its own profile drawn at its own time position

Scenario: Recorder limit
  Given the recorder covers fewer sessions than requested
  Then the composite is built from what exists and states the covered range explicitly

Scenario: Cold query stays within budget
  Given a 30-session composite request
  Then it is served from Parquet/DuckDB within 2 s and meta.sources reports parquet

Scenario: Composites accumulate, never average
  Given two sessions with known level volumes
  Then every composite level equals the exact sum of the contributing sessions and the composite POC is computed after summation

Scenario: Gap inside the look-back
  Given a recording gap inside the requested sessions
  Then the affected sessions are flagged and the composite states which days are missing rather than silently omitting them
```

## Technical notes / design
The merge is element-wise on sparse level dicts, which is why accumulation order is irrelevant and the result is exactly reproducible. Long look-backs stream results per session so the pane can render progressively and show progress; the composite POC/VA are computed only once all contributing sessions have landed, so the user never sees a POC that jumps as data arrives. Where the hot and cold tiers both cover part of a window, the hot tier wins for the overlapping range to avoid double counting, and `meta.sources` lists both.

## Test plan
Unit: element-wise merge, accumulate-not-average assertion, hot/cold overlap resolution, coverage computation. Integration: 30-session Parquet fixture with a deliberate gap; hot/cold boundary fixture. E2E: composite of 5 sessions; per-session multiples; look-back exceeding history shows a warning and still renders. Perf: 30-session composite p95 ≤ 2 s, recorded in the load report.

## Security notes
Look-back is bounded by `fixed_duration_minutes ≤ 10080` and the session-count cap; combined with T02's per-user cold-query concurrency limit this is the mitigation for cold-tier resource exhaustion — a 30-session DuckDB scan is the most expensive request in the market-data API and must not be issuable without limit. No user input reaches SQL unparameterised.

## Accessibility notes
The covered range and any missing sessions are stated in text and announced on load, never implied by a faded bar. Per-session multiples are individually labelled with their session date so the table alternative can group rows by session. The composite anchor picker is a grouped, labelled form with an explicit description of what each anchor changes.

## Performance notes
≤ 2 s for 30 sessions from the cold tier (US-VP-003 NFR); progressive per-session rendering so first paint is fast; merged profile respects the 5 000-row cap with LOD merging.

## Observability
`profile_composite_duration_ms{sessions}`, `profile_cold_query_duration_ms`, `profile_composite_sessions_missing`; analytics `profile.composite_lookback_changed`, `profile.multiples_toggled`.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All Gherkin scenarios covered by named automated tests.
- [ ] 2 s budget demonstrated on the 30-session fixture in CI's perf job.
- [ ] Coverage ≥85% backend / ≥80% frontend; axe-core green; design-qa sign-off; demoed.

`blocked_by`: **E19-S02** (period lifecycle and multi-instance panes), **E16** (recorder, retention and Parquet cold tier). Blocks **E19-S09** only informally (presets include composite anchors).

`feat/e19-composite-profiles`

title: TPO / market profile with 24-7 periods, initial balance and single prints
body:
## Context
Implements **US-VP-008 — TPO / market profile (Should)**: letter-based time-at-price with "a 24/7-appropriate period definition". Classic market profile assumes an RTH session; crypto has none, so `24-internal-schemas.md` §5.2 pins the adaptation: `tpo_period_min` (default 30) buckets, letters assigned `A…Z, a…z, AA…` by bucket index, TPO POC/VA computed with `tpo_count` in place of `volume`, UTC-anchored by default. The document is explicit that TPO and volume profiles **can disagree** (one huge print vs. many periods at a level) and that this is a feature. Note the roadmap's §11 descoping ladder lists "TPO/market-profile mode and composite profiles" as the **first** candidate to slip to R5 if R2 capacity is short — this story is therefore built to be independently deferrable, behind a feature flag, with no other VP story depending on it.

## Scope / Deliverables
- TPO accumulation in `ProfileEngine`: per-level `tpo_count` incremented once per bucket that touches the level regardless of volume; `tpo_period_minutes` configurable 1–240 (REST bound).
- `kind=tpo` on `GET /market/profile` and `profile.{symbol}.tpo` on WS.
- Letter rendering in the T04 plugin (**CMP-184** MarketProfileTpoPane): letters per price per period, letter size configurable (SCR-039), collapsing to blocks when letters fall below legibility size.
- TPO POC/VAH/VAL via **E19-S04**'s expansion algorithm over `tpo_count`, including the `two_row_tpo` option that exists precisely for reference-platform parity.
- **Initial balance**: the first N periods marked and their range labelled; N configurable.
- **Single prints**: rows touched by exactly one period highlighted with a glyph, toggleable.
- Overlay mode: TPO and volume profile drawn together on one price axis, since they intentionally disagree.
- Feature flag `profiles.tpo` so the mode can ship dark if R2 capacity is short.

## Out of scope
- RTH/overnight session semantics, open/close ranges and other equity-market profile conventions.
- TPO-based composites (composite is volume/delta in R2; TPO composites are a Could).
- Letter-based alerting — **E40**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: TPO built
  Given 30-minute TPO periods anchored to the configured day boundary
  Then letters accumulate per price per period and the profile shape is drawn

Scenario: Initial balance
  Then the first N periods are marked as the initial balance with its range labelled

Scenario: Single prints
  Then single-print rows are highlighted with a glyph and can be toggled off

Scenario: TPO and volume may disagree
  Given one very large print at a level touched by a single period
  Then the volume profile shows a high-volume level while the TPO profile shows a single print, and both are correct and can be overlaid

Scenario: Letters exceed the alphabet
  Given a session with more than 52 periods
  Then letters continue as AA, AB, ... deterministically and remain unique within the session

Scenario: Letters below legible size
  Given the period is dense enough that letters would render under the legibility threshold
  Then the profile collapses to blocks with the letter mapping still available on hover and in the table alternative
```

## Technical notes / design
TPO is a second counter on the **same** `ProfileLevel`, not a second engine — that is what lets the overlay be exactly row-aligned with the volume profile. Bucket membership is computed from the trade timestamp and the session anchor, so replay produces identical letters. Letter rendering reuses the SDF glyph atlas within the ≤3 text-draw-call budget; when letters are too small the plugin switches to the block path automatically, which also keeps the 5 000-row cap achievable. The `two_row_tpo` value-area variant is wired here because TPO is where parity with reference platforms is actually scrutinised.

## Test plan
Unit (≥85%): bucket assignment across the anchor boundary, letter sequence past Z and past z, `tpo_count` increment-once-per-bucket rule, IB range, single-print detection, TPO VA under both algorithms. Golden data: a fixture session with a published expected letter grid. E2E: TPO mode, IB labelling, single-print toggle, overlay with volume. Visual: golden images for letters and the collapsed block mode, both themes. Perf: TPO session render within the R4 budget at maximum period count.

## Security notes
`tpo_period_minutes` bounded 1–240 server-side — a 1-minute period over a week is the obvious amplification request and is covered by the existing window bounds and the cold-query concurrency limit. Read-only, `marketdata:read`. The feature flag is server-evaluated so a client cannot enable a dark mode by flipping local state.

## Accessibility notes
Letters are decorative encoding, not an accessible representation: the table alternative lists each price row with its period count, its letter set and IB/single-print membership, and POC/VAH/VAL are announced. The collapsed block mode keeps the letter mapping available on hover and in the table. Single prints and IB use glyph plus text, never colour alone. Letter size is user-configurable with a minimum that meets legibility guidance.

## Performance notes
TPO adds one integer per level per bucket — negligible engine cost. Render cost is dominated by letters; the automatic collapse to blocks keeps the ≤ 8 ms R4 budget and the ≤3 text draw calls intact at high density. Measured in the B-profile benchmark with a TPO case.

## Observability
`profile_tpo_periods{symbol}`, `profile_tpo_render_mode{letters|blocks}`, `profile_tpo_compute_duration_ms`; analytics `profile.mode_changed{mode=tpo}`, `profile.tpo_period_changed`, `profile.single_prints_toggled`, `profile.ib_periods_changed`.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All Gherkin scenarios covered by named automated tests; expected letter grid asserted against the fixture.
- [ ] Feature flag wired and defaulted per the R2 capacity decision.
- [ ] Coverage ≥85% engine / ≥80% frontend; axe-core green; screen-reader pass on the table alternative.
- [ ] Golden images approved; design-qa sign-off; demoed.

## Dependencies
`blocked_by`: **E19-S04** (value-area algorithm reused with `tpo_count`); requires **US-CHART-009** session anchoring from E12. Blocks nothing — deliberately, so it can be descoped to R5 per `30-release-roadmap.md` §11.

## Branch

title: Profile settings dialog and presets shared across instances (SCR-039)
body:
## Context
Implements **US-VP-009 — Profile panel settings & presets (Must)**. Nine stories' worth of knobs are worthless if switching analysis style takes a dozen clicks; the story's value is that one preset switches "period type, row size, value area %, VWAP overlay and node marking" together. The NFR extends it to the workspace layer: "presets stored per user and included in workspace export." The surface is **SCR-039 Profile settings dialog**.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **SCR-039** modal implementing the full SCR-038 settings list plus per-period colouring, "extend POC/VA lines to the right", "show developing VA" and composite period anchors: components **CMP-006** RadioGroup, **CMP-008** NumericStepperInput, **CMP-031** ColorSwatch/ThemeChip, **CMP-040** FormField, **CMP-043** Dialog, **CMP-065** FormSection, **CMP-228** PreviewTile.
- Live preview tile reflecting the pending settings before apply.
- Presets: save current settings as a named preset, apply to any profile instance for any symbol, rename/delete; shipped defaults incl. "session value".
- Persistence per user (workspace/pane settings payload per `21-database-schema.md` §3.8 `pane_settings` / `indicator_instances`) and inclusion in workspace export/import.
- Validation per SCR-039: VA % 1–100 in the UI clamped to the API's 50–95 with an explanatory message; custom range end after start; look-back longer than recorded history **warns** rather than blocks; row size smaller than tick size clamped to one tick with an explanation (US-VP-009 scenario).
- Reset-to-defaults.

## Out of scope
- The underlying computations each setting drives (owned by S01–S08).
- Global app settings and hotkeys — **SCR-110/111**, E-settings.
- Sharing presets between users — collaboration, R5.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Preset applied
  When I apply the "session value" preset
  Then period type, row size, value area %, VWAP overlay and node marking all switch together

Scenario: Save preset
  When I save current settings as a preset
  Then it is available to all profile instances for any symbol

Scenario: Invalid row size
  When the row size is smaller than the instrument tick size
  Then it is clamped to one tick with an explanatory message

Scenario: Look-back exceeds recorded history
  When a composite look-back longer than the recorded history is chosen
  Then a warning is shown and the dialog still applies, producing a profile that states its covered range

Scenario: Preview before apply
  Given pending changes in the dialog
  Then the preview tile reflects them and cancelling restores the previous settings exactly

Scenario: Presets survive export/import
  Given a workspace containing presets is exported and imported on another machine
  Then every preset reappears with identical values
```

## Technical notes / design
Settings are a single validated object per profile instance; a preset is that object minus instance-specific bindings (symbol, anchor timestamps), which is what makes "available for any symbol" true by construction. Re-bucketing on apply is worker-local (SCR-039 perf note: ≤ 300 ms from cached raw data) so the dialog feels instant and only a period change hits the network. UI-vs-API validation ranges deliberately differ (VA % 1–100 in the dialog per SCR-039, 50–95 at the API per OpenAPI): the dialog clamps and explains rather than silently accepting a value the server will reject.

## Test plan
Unit: settings schema validation, clamping and warning logic, preset serialisation, preview diffing, cancel-restores-exactly. E2E: apply a preset and assert every dependent control changed; save/rename/delete a preset; row-size clamp message; look-back warning; workspace export/import round-trip. Visual: golden images of the dialog in both themes. a11y: axe-core plus a keyboard-only traversal of the whole dialog.

## Security notes
Presets are per-user rows scoped by owner; a user cannot read or apply another user's preset (enforced server-side on the workspace/settings endpoints, not just by the UI). Imported workspace payloads are schema-validated and size-bounded before persistence — an imported workspace is untrusted input and is the injection vector worth guarding here. No secrets are ever stored in a preset.

## Accessibility notes
Grouped form controls with units in the label ("Value area %", "Row size (ticks)"); the mode selector is a radio group; each section has a description explaining what it changes. Focus is trapped in the dialog and returns to the invoking control on close; Esc cancels. Validation messages are associated with their fields and announced; warnings are distinguishable from errors by text, not colour. The preview tile has a text summary alternative.

## Performance notes
Row-size and period changes re-bucket from cached raw data in a worker in ≤ 300 ms for a session-length profile; composite look-backs show progress rather than blocking (SCR-039). Dialog open ≤ 80 ms.

## Observability
Analytics `profile.settings_changed{key}`, `profile.preset_applied{name}`, `profile.preset_saved`, `profile.settings_reset`. Metric `ui_profile_rebucket_duration_ms`.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All Gherkin scenarios covered by named automated tests.
- [ ] Workspace export/import round-trip test green.
- [ ] Coverage ≥80% frontend; axe-core green; keyboard-only and screen-reader pass on the dialog.
- [ ] Golden images approved; design-qa sign-off against the SCR-039 checklist; demoed.

## Dependencies
`blocked_by`: **E19-S02** (period types to configure), **E19-S04** (VA settings). Related: **E19-S03**, **E19-S05**, **E19-S08** contribute controls; the dialog degrades gracefully when the TPO flag is off.

title: SAST/DAST rules and CI security gates for the profile compute and read paths
body:
## Context
The planning brief requires SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Bandit), SCA, secrets scanning and DAST (OWASP ZAP) as standing gates, and `docs/plan/04-security-program.md` expects each epic to contribute the rules that encode *its* specific hazards. Generic rules will not catch the things that actually threaten profiles: string-built time-series queries against QuestDB or DuckDB, unbounded window handling, cost-unbounded cold-tier reads, error handlers that echo store details, and accumulation paths that are not keyed idempotently.

This ticket turns the `E19-X01` mitigations into automation that keeps enforcing them after the humans move to R3.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Custom Semgrep rules** in `security/semgrep/e19/`:
  - Ban string interpolation or f-strings in any QuestDB/DuckDB/SQL query construction inside the profile engine and market-data routers; require parameterised queries or the approved query builder.
  - Require every profile query path to pass through the bounded-window validator; flag any handler reading `from`/`to` without it.
  - Flag exception handlers in the market-data routers that serialise exception text, `repr`, or store client errors into responses instead of mapping to the documented error catalogue.
  - Flag accumulation code paths that mutate a period without a trade-id/sequence idempotency key.
  - Flag any profile endpoint or WS topic handler lacking an explicit permission declaration (`marketdata:read`).
- **CodeQL / Bandit configuration** extended to cover the profile engine package and the market-data API module, with the relevant query packs enabled and findings failing the build at the agreed severity.
- **DAST (OWASP ZAP) profile** for the read surface: an authenticated scan context for `/api/v1/market/profile` seeded with the OpenAPI definition, plus a WS-aware scripted check for `profile.*` subscription authorization, with a tuned false-positive baseline committed so the scan is actionable rather than noisy.
- **CI gates**: rules wired into the existing security workflow, scoped so they run on PRs touching the profile engine, market-data routers or WS routing; documented severity thresholds for blocking versus reporting.
- **Rule tests**: each custom rule ships with a positive and a negative fixture proving it fires on the hazard and does not fire on the approved pattern.
- Short **runbook section** in `docs/security/ci-gates.md` explaining each E19 rule, why it exists (linked to the threat it mitigates) and how to fix a violation, so a developer hitting the gate is unblocked without asking Security.

## Out of scope
- Container and dependency scanning (Trivy, pip-audit, npm audit) - programme-level, already enforced by E03/E43.
- Runtime WAF or network controls; infrastructure hardening.
- The abuse-case suite itself (`E19-X02`), which is dynamic testing rather than static analysis.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Rules fire on their hazards
  Given the positive fixtures for each custom rule
  When the security workflow runs
  Then every rule reports a finding on its positive fixture and reports nothing on its negative fixture

Scenario: A string-built store query cannot merge
  Given a pull request that builds a QuestDB query by interpolating the symbol parameter
  When CI runs
  Then the security job fails and names the rule and the file and line

Scenario: Failure case - an unvalidated window handler is caught
  Given a new profile handler that reads from and to without the bounded-window validator
  Then the rule fires and the PR is blocked until the validator is applied or an explicit reviewed suppression with a reason is added

Scenario: DAST scan is actionable
  Given the ZAP scan against the staging profile endpoint
  When it completes
  Then it produces zero unreviewed high findings and its baseline file explains every suppressed alert

Scenario: Edge case - suppression requires justification
  Given a developer adds a nosemgrep or equivalent suppression
  Then CI requires an inline reason and a linked ticket, and an unjustified suppression fails the build
```

## Technical notes / design
- Rules are scoped by path so they are precise and cheap; a broad repository-wide ban on string queries would drown teams in false positives and be disabled within a sprint, which is the usual failure mode of security gates.
- The bounded-window rule is written against the *validator symbol* rather than a pattern of arithmetic, so it survives refactoring of the limit logic and only requires the call site to be present.
- The DAST context uses the OpenAPI file directly, so new parameters are scanned automatically; the WS check is scripted separately because ZAP does not natively reason about the subscription protocol.
- Severity thresholds are agreed with DevSecOps up front and recorded, so a blocking finding is never a surprise negotiated during a release crunch.

## Test plan
- Rule fixtures run in CI as part of the security workflow's own self-test.
- The DAST profile is exercised once against staging during this ticket and then nightly; the baseline is reviewed whenever the contract changes.
- A deliberate regression PR (interpolated query) is opened on a scratch branch to prove the gate blocks, with evidence attached.

## Security notes
- Scanner credentials and ZAP contexts are stored as CI secrets; the committed context file contains no tokens.
- Findings are triaged per `04-security-program.md`; high severity blocks merge, medium is time-boxed with an owner, low is tracked.
- The rules themselves are reviewed by the Security engineer, since a poorly written rule creates false confidence, which is worse than no rule.
- Suppressions are auditable: every suppression carries a reason and a ticket, and a periodic report lists all active suppressions on E19 paths.

## Accessibility notes
- Not directly applicable (CI tooling). Indirectly, the error-catalogue rule protects the accessible error states on `SCR-038` by preventing raw exception text - which is neither announced well nor comprehensible - from reaching the UI.

## Performance notes
- The added security jobs must not extend PR feedback time beyond the agreed CI budget; path scoping and rule caching keep the incremental cost under the target, and the added duration is measured and recorded in the ticket.
- The nightly DAST scan runs off the critical path so it never gates interactive development.

## Observability
- Security job results are published to the programme security dashboard with per-epic attribution, so E19's gate health is visible alongside other epics.
- Suppression counts and finding trends are reported, making a slow erosion of the gates detectable rather than invisible.

## Definition of Done
- Custom rules, CodeQL/Bandit configuration and the ZAP profile merged and running in CI.
- Every rule has passing positive and negative fixtures; the deliberate regression PR demonstrated to block.
- `docs/security/ci-gates.md` updated with the E19 section including fix guidance.
- Baseline reviewed and zero unreviewed high findings; DevSecOps and Security engineer approval recorded.

## Dependencies
- `E19-X01` (threats the rules encode), `E19-T01`/`E19-T02` (the code paths and the bounded-window validator to reference).
- Existing security workflow and scanner infrastructure from E03/E04.

## Branch
`chore/e19-security-ci-gates`

## References

- `docs/plan/01-sdlc-and-branching.md` (required checks)
- `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml` `/market/profile` (DAST seed)
- `docs/security/threat-models/e19-profiles.md`
- `docs/plan/20-architecture.md` (M9 order-flow engines, M23 gateway)

- Ban string interpolation or f-strings in any QuestDB/DuckDB/SQL query construction inside the profile engine and market-data routers; require parameterised queries or the approved query builder.

- Flag exception handlers in the market-data routers that serialise exception text, `repr`, or store client errors into responses instead of mapping to the documented error catalogue.

title: Security review and sign-off for E19 profiles
body:
## Context
`docs/plan/02-definition-of-ready-done.md` section 2.2 requires, for any epic labelled `security`, a finalised STRIDE model, triaged findings and a written sign-off from the Security engineer before the epic can be Done - and `docs/plan/30-release-roadmap.md` gates R2 on its epics' exits. E19 publishes values that automation will trade against, so its security posture is a prerequisite for the alerting and rule work in later trains, not an afterthought that can be cleaned up during hardening.

This ticket is the white-box counterpart to the black-box abuse testing: a human review of the profile code paths against the threat model, followed by the formal sign-off artefact.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **White-box security review** of the profile implementation:
  - Query construction in the profile engine and market-data routers (parameterisation, symbol validation against the instrument registry, window bounding, row caps).
  - Idempotency and ordering of accumulation (trade-id keying, out-of-order and duplicate handling, period assignment from timestamps, clamping of implausible timestamps).
  - Cache and store trust: the 5 s flush, restart rebuild, `metadata_version` invalidation, and what is assumed about store integrity.
  - Authorization on both transports: `marketdata:read` enforcement on REST and on WS subscribe, symbol allow-list handling, revocation on token expiry, and preset/workspace ownership checks.
  - Error handling and information disclosure across the profile surface, verified against the documented error catalogue.
  - Resource governance: bounded windows, row caps, subscription quotas, rate limits and their defaults as shipped (not as designed).
  - Dependency review of any new library introduced by the epic (statistics, compression, columnar readers), including licence and maintenance posture.
- **Findings triage**: all findings from `E19-X01` (model), `E19-X02` (abuse cases), `E19-X03` (SAST/DAST) and the security-relevant results of `E19-Q05` (chaos) consolidated into one list with severity, disposition and owner.
- **Sign-off document** `docs/security/signoff/e19-profiles.md`: scope reviewed, method, findings summary, residual risks with Owner acceptance where applicable, items deferred to the R4 pen-test scope, and an explicit verdict.
- **Handover notes** to E40 (alerts) and the rule engine: the integrity and repudiation guarantees the profile metrics do and do not provide, so consuming epics design accordingly rather than assuming.

## Out of scope
- Remediation work itself, which lands on the owning engineering tickets; this review blocks on remediation but does not perform it.
- Programme-level pen-test execution (E43) - this ticket contributes scope to it.
- Infrastructure and host hardening (E03/E43).

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every threat has a verified control
  Given docs/security/threat-models/e19-profiles.md
  When the review walks each mitigation to the shipped code and configuration
  Then each is confirmed implemented with a code or config reference, or is recorded as a finding

Scenario: Findings are consolidated and dispositioned
  Given findings from E19-X01, E19-X02, E19-X03 and E19-Q05
  When they are triaged
  Then every finding has a severity, an owner and a disposition of fixed, accepted with Owner sign-off, or deferred with a target train

Scenario: Failure case - an open high finding blocks sign-off
  Given an open high-severity finding that symbol input reaches a store query unparameterised
  When sign-off is attempted
  Then the verdict is "not signed", the E19 epic and E19-Q08 are blocked, and no conditional sign-off is issued

Scenario: Edge case - a residual risk is accepted explicitly
  Given the store-integrity assumption cannot be fully enforced in R2
  Then the residual risk is written in plain language, accepted by the Owner with a date, and handed to the R4 pen-test scope

Scenario: Consuming epics receive the guarantees in writing
  When the sign-off is published
  Then it states what integrity and auditability guarantees profile metrics provide, and E40 and the rule engine epics are linked to it
```

## Technical notes / design
- The review is performed against the release-candidate build, not against the design: defaults as shipped (actual limit values, actual quota numbers) are what get recorded, because a control configured to an ineffective value is not a control.
- Reviewer independence: the reviewer is the Security engineer, not an E19 implementer; the order-flow lead attends as an explainer rather than a reviewer.
- The handover notes are the highest-value durable output - later epics will build automated trading behaviour on these metrics, and the failure mode to avoid is an unstated assumption that a profile value is tamper-evident when it is only tamper-resistant.
- Deferred items are written directly in pen-test-scope language so E43 can adopt them without re-analysis.

## Test plan
- Verification is evidence-based: each control confirmed by a passing test from `E19-X02`, `E19-Q02` or `E19-Q05`, or by a manual check recorded in the document; "reviewed the code and it looks fine" is not accepted as evidence for a rated threat.
- Re-verification of every fixed finding on the candidate build before the verdict is issued.

## Security notes
- Follows the `04-security-program.md` sign-off template; the verdict feeds the programme risk register and the R2 PRR.
- Sensitive finding detail remains in the private security tracker; the public document carries summaries and references.
- The review explicitly checks that nothing in the epic introduced a dependency on privileges beyond `marketdata:read`, keeping the read surface's blast radius minimal ahead of live enablement.

## Accessibility notes
- Confirms that every security-driven user-facing state introduced by remediation (rate limited, unauthorized, validation error) is present in the `SCR-038` state list and was covered by the `E19-Q06` audit, so security fixes cannot quietly create inaccessible dead ends.

## Performance notes
- Records the shipped values of the resource-governance limits and confirms they match the numbers measured in `E19-Q04`, so the security review and the performance report cannot claim different ceilings.

## Observability
- Confirms the detection telemetry from `E19-X01` exists in staging and that alerts are configured for the security-relevant signals (rejected windows, quota rejections, authorization failures, rebuild failures).
- Any missing detection is a finding with an ops owner, not a documentation note.

**Repo paths to create/modify**
Base area for `cross-cutting`: cross-package: apps/web, services/api, packages/chart-engine as named in Scope
- **White-box security review** of the profile implementation:
- Query construction in the profile engine and market-data routers (parameterisation, symbol validation against the instrument registry, window bounding, row caps).
- Idempotency and ordering of accumulation (trade-id keying, out-of-order and duplicate handling, period assignment from timestamps, clamping of implausible timestamps).
- Cache and store trust: the 5 s flush, restart rebuild, `metadata_version` invalidation, and what is assumed about store integrity.
- Authorization on both transports: `marketdata:read` enforcement on REST and on WS subscribe, symbol allow-list handling, revocation on token expiry, and preset/workspace ownership checks.
